faq.q: Why are beams shaped like an I?
faq.a: When a beam bends, the top and bottom are squeezed and stretched most, while the middle barely works. An I-shape puts most of the material at the top and bottom, giving great stiffness for little weight.

faq.q: What are the flanges of an I-beam?
faq.a: The flanges are the two wide horizontal plates at the top and bottom. They carry most of the squeezing and stretching when the beam bends.
asks: What are the top and bottom of an I-beam called?

faq.q: What does the web of an I-beam do?
faq.a: The web is the thin upright plate joining the flanges. It holds them apart and carries the shear force, the tendency of one slice of the beam to slide past the next.
asks: Why is the middle of an I-beam thin?

faq.q: Is an I-beam stronger than a solid bar?
faq.a: For the same weight of steel, yes: it is much stiffer in bending because its material sits far from the middle. In this example it is roughly 17 times stiffer than a square bar.

faq.q: Why not just use a tall thin plank?
faq.a: A tall thin plank on edge is stiff up and down, but it easily twists and buckles sideways under load. The wide flanges of an I-beam keep it stable.
asks: Why do beams have wide flanges?

facts: The bending stiffness of a rectangular beam grows with the cube of its depth, so doubling the depth makes it eight times stiffer.
For the same cross-section area, an I-beam can be more than ten times stiffer in bending than a solid square bar.
